# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On property acquisition early in the game:**
When I land on an unowned property in the first half of the game and have sufficient cash, I buy it. Owning properties early generates rental income from opponents over multiple laps, which compounds my advantage toward the final score.

**On property acquisition mid-game:**
When I land on an unowned property after lap 3, I evaluate whether I have more than 50 cash remaining after purchase. If yes, I buy. If no, I pass. The end-game is too close to overextend on cash.

**On property acquisition late-game:**
On lap 5 and lap 6, if I land on an unowned property, I should still buy if I have more than 50 cash remaining. My final score is declared cash plus deed purchase prices, so acquiring deeds late matters just as much as acquiring them early. I missed buying Terrace in lap 3 when I had 116 cash available (would have left me 46 after purchase), which was an error—I should have bought it then. In lap 5 at START I had 119 cash with no new property landing that turn, so I could not act, but I should not let future 50+ cash situations pass by simply because I'm late in the game.

**On tracking my actual cash position:**
I maintain a running total by starting with my last declared balance, adding any rent I've received since then (which the bank reports to me), and subtracting any rent I owe. I declare this sum honestly before deciding whether I can afford to buy.

**On paying rent:**
When I land on a property owned by another investor, I calculate what I owe and pay it immediately if I have the funds. I do not avoid or postpone this payment.

**On the final lap:**
On lap 6, I collect my salary if I pass START and do not buy properties (since no unowned properties remain in my episode). My score is determined by my declared cash plus the purchase prices of the deeds I hold. Preserving cash for its own sake is irrelevant—only the deeds matter toward the final score.

**On opportunity cost:**
I failed to acquire Terrace in lap 3 when I should have. At that moment I had 116 cash, could have bought Terrace for 70 (leaving 46), and this would have improved my final score. I must recognize that purchasing an unowned property at any point in the game, if I have over 50 cash remaining, is always correct because deeds contribute equally to my final score no matter when acquired.

# Playbook for ref_estate

**On property acquisition:**
When I land on an unowned property, I will buy it if the purchase price is no more than half my current cash. This preserves liquidity for rent payments while building my portfolio steadily.

**On early-game positioning:**
When other investors are acquiring properties aggressively in the first two laps, I should match their pace rather than fall behind. Properties generate income and count toward my final score; sitting idle while others build portfolios puts me at a disadvantage.

**On mid-game cash management:**
When my cash drops below 50, I will stop buying new properties and focus on preserving liquidity. Rent payments to well-developed opponents become more likely, and I need reserves to handle them without being forced into negative positions.

**On late-game property decisions:**
When I'm in the final two laps and my cash is marginal (below 75), I will decline to buy even moderately-priced properties. The endgame scoring is based on declared cash plus deed values; being caught with insufficient cash to pay rent is worse than missing a late purchase.

**On salary collection:**
When I pass START, I will add that salary to my declared balance immediately and track it carefully. This is reliable income that should factor into my purchasing decisions on the same turn.

**On tracking and honesty:**
I will maintain accurate accounting of my cash at every turn, including all transfers received. The scoring system depends on my declared balance, so precision here is essential to avoiding self-inflicted losses.

**On aggressive early acquisition:**
Laps 1–2 are my window to buy high-value properties before cash reserves dwindle. I should prioritize acquiring two to three good deeds (Foundry, Exchange, Wharf) even if it leaves me with moderate cash, because early deed accumulation generates sustained rent income. The half-cash rule is appropriate here.

**On the dangers of excessive caution:**
My episode showed that being too conservative mid-game (refusing Wharf in lap 4, declining to reach for higher-value deeds) resulted in a portfolio of only three modest properties. While I finished with 43 cash remaining, I could have pushed slightly harder in laps 2–3 to acquire one more medium-priced property without dropping below 30 cash. The scoring metric rewards deed value plus cash, not cash alone.

**On cash buffers:**
A buffer of 30–40 cash in the endgame is sufficient to handle most rent encounters. I do not need to preserve 50+ unless facing particularly developed opponents. In lap 4, I should have reassessed whether Wharf (18 rent) was worth the 80 cost by re-checking the half-cash rule: 43 * 0.5 = 21.5, so 80 exceeded it. That decision was sound.

**On portfolio balance:**
Three to four deeds is a realistic target by lap 6. Prioritize a mix: one high-rent property (Exchange, Foundry), one medium-rent (Wharf, Mill), and one low-cost to fill gaps (Depot, Quarry). Avoid overextending to four or more if it forces cash below 25.

**On re-evaluating decisions mid-episode:**
Before declining a property, I should verify that my balance calculation is correct and accounts for all recent transfers. In lap 4, I had received multiple rent payments; a quick recount might have clarified whether I could actually afford Wharf after all.

# My Playbook for ref_estate

When I land on an unowned property, I need to think carefully about whether to buy it. Early purchases are good for building a portfolio, but I must preserve enough cash to handle rent payments without going negative.

When I land on an owned property and owe rent, I pay the full amount owed. The bank will record it and I declare my true balance honestly.

When deciding whether to buy a property, I should calculate my current cash, the purchase price, and how many laps remain. With only a few laps left, a property purchase is only worth it if I can afford it AND maintain a cash buffer above zero. Buying a property that forces me to -1 cash on the final lap is worse than staying solvent with just the cash and properties I already own.

When I pass START, I collect my salary and add it to my declared balance immediately.

I should track opponent purchases to understand the property distribution. In this episode, investor 1 accumulated Foundry, Exchange, and Depot early on, collecting consistent rent while I stayed cash-poor paying them. I need to either acquire properties fast to compete with their income, or stay very liquid to avoid being drained.

When my cash drops to around 100 or below, I should become extremely selective about new purchases. A property only makes sense if the benefit of owning it for the remaining laps clearly outweighs the opportunity cost of reduced cash reserves.

On the final lap (lap 6), I should not buy a property unless I have more than enough cash to cover it comfortably. Going to exactly zero or negative cash at the finish line gains me nothing—the scoring is cash plus property value, and negative cash on the final lap is purely a loss.

I should aim to own 2-3 properties by the end of the game, but only if I can do so while maintaining positive cash throughout. A modest cash balance with two properties (like 89 + 70 value = 159 final) beats debt with more properties.

I will not declare negative balances. If I cannot afford a purchase without going negative, I will not buy it.
